title: Augmedics (Disrupt SF 2017 final)

transcript.text: Hi, I'm Nissan. I'm the founder and CEO of FOGMEDIX. I want to talk about X-ray vision. And I mean real X-ray vision, when you can actually see through walls or even inside a human body. Imagine what if surgeons had X-ray vision and they could see their patients anatomy through skin and tissue. Cool, huh? Could be great for spine surgery, for example, where surgeons need to drill holes and insert screws into the spine.

When surgeons drill holes and insert the screws to the spine, it needs to be very careful not to breach the bone or, God forbid, not to damage the spinal cord. The problem is that you cannot really see where the screw goes inside the vertebrae, right? In fact, although the spine surgeons are very experienced, up to 23% of all the screws placed during spine surgery are malpositioned and in some cases it can even make the patient paralyzed.

So what can surgeons do? Well, they can use a GPS-like surgical navigation systems that can help them to guide their instrument directly to the correct place. Now please take a look at these pictures. Well, the surgeons are looking at why are they facing away from the patient? What you are seeing here in this picture is the navigated spine surgery. Not a single person in the OR is actually looking at the patient during the procedure because all the navigated information is projected on the distance screen.

Just try to imagine that at the most critical moment when the surgeon actually drills inside the vertebra, you need to take his head off the patient and look aside on the distant screen to navigate. All the current solutions for navigation are uncomfortable for the surgeons, they're not intuitive and that is the reason why surgeons are not using navigation systems so often. So we asked ourselves how can we help surgeons use navigation systems and also look at their patient at the same time.

We realized that the best way to do it is to give surgeons and x-ray vision so they can see the patient's anatomy through the skin and tissue. I'm happy to say that after three years of work we have accomplished that by developing the visor, a see-through device that goes beyond the limitation of our eyes and beyond the complications of any other existing technology. With our patented device we are able to project the patient anatomy in real time directly onto the surgeon's retina with surgical precision and with outstanding depth perception.

Now let's switch to the demo and I'll show you how it works. Ron, step over here. I'll explain to you what you're gonna see here. So this is Ron here. This is a live demo of our system. This is a human phantom which represents the human body with a spine inside. I can show you that there is a spine over here as well. Just a few seconds.

Picture is stuck. Yeah, okay. So the video feed here is stuck, but the system is still running, so you can see it here. So anyway, this is a spine phantom. What we have inside is a phantom spine of a human being. And before the surgery, we placed a microinform in the patient. We do the whole Surgical navigation, the workflow is the same as all other navigation systems.

We place a marker on the patient and then we scan the patient just before the surgery. And then we take the CT scans, we build a 3D model of the CT scans and we register this 3D model to the real patient lying on the surgical table. Then we project the 3D model directly to the surgeon's retina, right and left, so we can see a true 3D spine model of the patient in a very good depth perception.

As you can see, there's a tool also that we can track. There's the tracking system, very accurate, and the tool can even be guided inside the patient's anatomy so you can see, the surgeon can see exactly where he's aiming for. Thank you. Let's switch back to the presentation. So let's talk a bit about our business. Surgical navigation market is estimated to reach $900 million a year. Our business model is to integrate the visor into existing surgical navigation systems and medical imaging systems.

And we already signed strategic partnership with several global leaders that will eventually sell our system together with their system. In the next few months we plan to start our clinical trials and by Q1 2019 we plan to commercialize the product. So if you're interested in having the visor in your operating room, please contact us at ogmedics.com. Thank you. Alright, judges.

brief.headline: Dig deeper: the problem is real, but the 'X-ray vision' pitch drifted into a standard CT-overlay navigation workflow, and the partnership-based go-to-market, patent and regulatory timeline are all unverified.
brief.summary: Augmedics (pitching as FOGMEDIX) is building an AR visor that projects a CT-derived 3D spine model onto the surgeon's retina so they can navigate while looking at the patient. The problem framing held up: spine navigation exists, and pedicle screw malposition of up to 23% is supported by independent studies (other studies report roughly 5-15%). The $900M market figure only matches the spine-only navigation segment (about $896M), while the broad surgical navigation market is closer to $10B. The 'real X-ray vision' framing weakened live: the founder described a pre-op CT scan registered to the patient via a marker, with a 'same as all other navigation' workflow, and the demo video froze. The business depends on partner integrations, signed deals with unnamed 'global leaders', a patent, and clinical trials leading to a Q1 2019 launch, none of which is evidenced.
strengths: Real, quantified clinical problem: up to 23% pedicle screw malposition is supported by independent studies, and navigation exists but forces surgeons to look at a distant screen
Clear wedge: spine navigation, where the $900M market figure matches the spine-only segment (about $896M)
Integrate-with-incumbents model avoids competing head-on with existing navigation and imaging vendors
Live demo with tool tracking on a spine phantom, though it was only partially visible

red_flags.text: The 'real X-ray vision / see inside the body' claim is overstated: live he described a pre-op CT model registered to the patient with a marker, not live imaging. He also mentioned a marker placed in the patient, and the claim of real-time projection with surgical precision and depth perception has no accuracy or latency data.

Differentiation is unclear: he said all current navigation is uncomfortable and unintuitive, then said the workflow is the same as all other systems. The only edge is heads-up display ergonomics, and the claim that surgeons underuse navigation because of ergonomics is unsupported.
The go-to-market depends on integrating with incumbents' systems, but the strategic partnerships with 'several global leaders' are unnamed and unverified, and their scope and obligations are unknown.
The demo video froze and the claim that the system was still running was not shown. The demo used a phantom, with no cadaver or clinical evidence.

The timeline is aggressive and unevidenced: clinical trials in a few months and commercial launch by Q1 2019 for a new AR medical device, with the patent and three-year development claims unverified. The market size is also only valid if it means spine navigation, not the broad market (about $10B).

questions: Who are the strategic partners, what exactly is signed (integration, distribution, exclusivity), and are they committing engineering or sales resources?
What is the measured registration accuracy (target registration error in mm) and latency, how do you handle patient movement after registration, and how much of the demo was live versus pre-rendered?
What exactly is the marker, is it implanted or invasive, and has it been tested or approved for use in patients?
What is the regulatory pathway (FDA 510(k) or de novo, CE), where are you today, and what is the realistic timeline to first trial and to Q1 2019 launch?
If the workflow is the same as existing navigation, what concretely makes this more intuitive, and what does the patent cover given existing AR headsets and navigation systems?

Said he placed a 'microinform' (apparently a marker) in the patient before surgery, which implies prior preparation not mentioned earlier.
Said all current navigation is uncomfortable and unintuitive, then said the workflow is the same as all other navigation systems.
